title: Sikh Truck Driver Stabbed 17 Times at Wyoming Rest Stop, Suspect Charged
excerpt: The 28-year-old Sacramento driver was followed into a restroom at the Bitter Creek Rest Area along I-80 in the early hours of Sept. 13 and airlifted to a Casper hospital; Andrew Kris Bzdak, 45, was arrested and charged with attempted first-degree murder.
body:
• A Sikh truck driver from Sacramento, identified only as Singh, was stabbed 17 times in a restroom at the Bitter Creek Rest Area along Interstate 80 in Sweetwater County, Wyoming, in the early hours of Sunday, Sept. 13.
  • Wyoming Highway Patrol arrested 45-year-old Andrew Kris Bzdak within hours and charged him with attempted first-degree murder; charging documents did not state a motive.
  • A Hispanic family at the rest area heard Singh's cries, followed the attacker's truck east on I-80 and relayed identifying details to police, leading to Bzdak's arrest near Rawlins.
  • The attack came days after the Department of Homeland Security posted — and then deleted — an AI-generated graphic mocking a Sikh "Mr Singh," drawing condemnation from Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Sikh advocacy groups.

A Sikh truck driver from the Sacramento area is recovering in a Wyoming hospital after being stabbed 17 times inside a restroom at a highway rest area early Sunday morning, an attack that has rattled the South Asian community across the United States.

The 28-year-old driver, who asked to be identified only by his surname Singh out of concern for his safety, told NPR he was driving toward Pennsylvania when he pulled into the Bitter Creek Rest Area along Interstate 80 in Sweetwater County around 3 a.m. He had stopped at the rest area many times before without incident. As he walked into the restroom, he sensed another man following behind him.

"I don't know why this happened," Singh said from his hospital room. "I don't know why they attack[ed] me."

Singh said the man began beating him without warning or provocation, then pulled out a knife and stabbed him repeatedly in the neck, chest, arms and ribs. After the attacker fled, Singh staggered outside and collapsed on the pavement. He was airlifted to Wyoming Medical Center in Casper with multiple lacerations and injuries to his chest and ribs, and remained hospitalised as of Wednesday night, according to NPR.

"They [gave] me the second life."

— Singh, describing the Hispanic family at the rest area who aided him and alerted police

Suspect Arrested After Bystanders Followed Truck

Law enforcement arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak, 45, within about 90 minutes of the attack and charged him with attempted first-degree murder, according to charging documents first reported by Cowboy State Daily. The documents did not state a motive for the attack, according to NPR's reporting.

Camera footage from a nearby parked truck showed Singh walking into the restroom, followed by a man in a black sweater and jeans later identified as Bzdak, who ran out of the bathroom less than a minute later and back to his truck, according to Land Line Media. The same family that found Singh told investigators they heard grunting and screaming from the restroom, then followed Bzdak's tractor-trailer east on I-80, photographing the trailer and relaying identifying information to police. Wyoming Highway Patrol deputies spotted the truck around 5 a.m. near Rawlins, roughly 70 miles east of the attack, and Bzdak was taken into custody without incident.

The Sweetwater County Sheriff's Office and the local prosecutor did not immediately respond to requests for comment, according to NPR.

Context & Background

The stabbing came days after the Department of Homeland Security posted an AI-generated graphic targeting a Sikh man identified as "Mr Singh" as part of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, according to Mint and other reports. The post carried the caption "Get off our roads. You don't know how to drive Mr Singh" and told the character to "self-deport or find out," drawing accusations of stereotyping from members of the South Asian community. DHS later deleted the post following criticism from lawmakers and advocacy groups.

Jasjit Singh Dhanoa, director of legal services at the Jakara Movement, spoke with the injured driver, according to a report in fact.net.in. Sikh groups and the Hindu American Foundation condemned the attack, linking it to rising anti-Sikh profiling concerns.

Impact & Analysis

U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.) said he was "horrified" by the attack and tied it to growing hostility toward Sikh and South Asian Americans. "Those spreading this hate, including officials in our own federal government, need to stop. Those who turn it into violence must be held accountable," he said in a statement. "And all of us need to stand together against both."

For many in the Sikh American community, the attack underscored the risks faced by drivers who are highly visible on the job — turbaned Sikh men are a familiar presence on America's highways, where thousands work as long-haul truckers. Community leaders said the DHS post had already stoked fears that anti-Sikh rhetoric from official channels could encourage harassment of drivers; the Wyoming attack, whatever its motive proves to be, has deepened those fears. In California's Sacramento area, where the victim lives, Sikh community members told Fox40 they were concerned about a pattern of rising violence.

What's Next

Bzdak remains in custody on the attempted first-degree murder charge. Investigators have not publicly identified a motive, and the Sweetwater County prosecutor's office has not said whether hate-crime enhancements are under consideration. Sikh advocacy groups are pressing law enforcement to investigate the attack as a possible hate crime, while the victim continues to recover at Wyoming Medical Center.
nri_angle: A Sikh long-haul trucker from California's diaspora community was nearly killed on a U.S. highway days after federal immigration rhetoric mocked a turbaned Sikh driver, forcing Sikh Americans to confront the physical risks of anti-South Asian hostility.
author: Diaspora Desk
